topics.topic: Haa - the letter and, far more, the SOUND. Four connecting forms, identical to jiim but with no dot at all, then close to fifteen minutes of pure pronunciation coaching: the constriction is at the epiglottis, mid-throat, tongue pulled slightly back but RELAXED, no vocal-cord vibration, air forced through a partly closed throat. She had them put a hand on the throat to feel the difference from English h, and gave two physical analogies - the breath you use to fog a mirror or your glasses before wiping them, and the 'aah' a Syrian makes over hot sweet tea. Drilled through real words rather than syllables: Habiib, baHth, SabaaH, Hisaan, Haafila, Hadiid, Haliib, Hibr, and the minimal-pair trap naHla (bee) against naxla (palm tree), which she returned to three separate times because the class kept sliding the constriction up the throat into khaa

Connecting and STACKING jiim / Haa / Khaa, which is where she broke with the book. All three are one shape distinguished only by dot position (jiim one dot under, Haa none, khaa one dot on top), and all three drop below the line, so a word that starts with one wrecks your baseline. The book's fix is to start on the line and climb; she said outright she does not like that and teaches stacking the following letter on top instead - 'I think they look nicer for the handwriting' - while allowing both as correct. Worked live: taaj, baab, and hijaab (Haa + jiim + alif + baa), which is the hard case because two below-the-line letters stack in a row. Then a dot-placement rule for stacked letters: push the dot toward the right so the reader knows it belongs to the FIRST letter, not the second. Closed the hour with drills 1 and 2 from the homework worked at the board by students

Homework 3 and the unit 2 oral assessment, walked through on screen item by item - the densest logistics block of the semester so far. She opened Canvas and Lingco side by side and pointed at each drill. For the oral assessment she played the recording live, demonstrated recording her own answer, and then answered the 'can I capture her voice too' question with a workaround. Both deadlines were stated outright at the top of the hour

Khaa - forms (one dot on TOP) and pronunciation, which she called the easy one of the three because English speakers already make it: 'it's like clearing your throat'. Sound is from the soft palate, back of the throat but HIGH, versus Haa which is the same region but low. Drilled with xawx, baTTiix, xubz, xass (lettuce, which the book's picture makes look like a house), and the naHiil / naxiil pair - thin person versus palm trees. Ended with one vocabulary word she ordered onto the list: taHt, 'under', taught against taxt, 'bed', the two differing only by the dot

announcements.text: HOMEWORK 3 IS DUE TOMORROW, Friday 2026-09-11. Stated in the opening plan for the day: 'First, we're going to talk about your homework that's due tomorrow.' The required (bold) items are unit 3 drills 1, 2 and 5 (listen on Lingco, write the words by hand), drill 3 (answered on Lingco - listen to a word and pick which of the three new letters it contains), and drill 4, the letter-connection drill, written on paper and photographed to Canvas. Unit 2 is finished except for the oral assessment.

ORAL ASSESSMENT (unit 2, drill 15) IS DUE TUESDAY 2026-09-15 BY END OF DAY, recorded on Lingco. 'We're going to talk about oral assessment that's due Tuesday, okay? Tuesday by the end of the day.' Format: a recorded conversation with a woman who asks a question then pauses for your answer, or greets you and pauses for your question back. She played it through in class - the prompts are the unit 2 greeting script (ahlan, ana ismi Dina / shu ismak, min ayna anti, ana min Suuriya, tasharrafna).

SHAMI ONLY on the oral assessment - do NOT also record the Egyptian track. Asked directly by Parker: 'do you want us to do the Egyptian and the Shami? No, just the Shami, just the Shami, no need for both of them.' Her reason is that Shami is the closest dialect to Fusha. Pick the male or female speaker track to match your own gender, because the speaker addresses you gendered. You may answer in either Shami or Fusha, whichever is comfortable.

A grading rule that applies to EVERY oral assessment this semester, not just this one: answer in complete sentences. 'always answer in any oral assessment, not just this one, any oral assessment, always answer with a full sentence. So when she said, don't say America, no, I want the whole sentence.' She contrasted it with speech among friends, where dropping words is fine. Unlimited attempts are allowed - record, listen back, and redo it if you do not like it.

Workaround she demonstrated live for the oral assessment: record the prompt audio on your PHONE, pause the phone while you answer, so that her voice and yours land in one file. 'In this case, it's better because I will hear her speaking and you speaking together.' She tested recording directly in Lingco on the class machine and only her own voice came through. She then said it is optional - 'If it's too hard for you to use your phone, that's fine, I'll manage.'

Photo-submission rules for handwritten drills, repeated from earlier weeks and expanded: shoot PORTRAIT, not landscape (Canvas now lets her rotate, but rotating can block her from annotating the page, and then she will make you retake it); and NAME each image file after the drill it contains. She thanked whoever started doing that: 'I would see the title of the picture and I would know right away this is drill one or two or three... That was very easier for me to grade.' Multiple short drills may share one page if it stays readable, but a long drill gets its own page.

DRILL 16 IS NOT REQUIRED but she pushed it hard - it is the reading-fluency drill and she deliberately left it unbolded. 'During 16, I did not, I did not put it in bold. But I highly recommend that you go through these drills in order to improve. So drill 16 will help you with the reading skills.' With three more letters in hand the possible combinations jump, which is exactly why she raised it now.

SLANG IS NOT ON THE EXAM. She opened the hour on student request with Levantine slang (shu fi ma fi, kiif Haalak / kiif Haalik, yalla) and when asked whether it could be tested said 'No, no, those are just extra. If you want to learn it, learn it. If you don't want to, that's fine.' This is her second week of teaching extra-curricular slang; treat it as culture, not as testable vocabulary.

At-home pronunciation practice, assigned without a date: the remaining Haa and Khaa words in the book were left undone in class deliberately - 'at home, we still have few more words, but at home.' Her method, stated explicitly: play the word on Lingco, say it, record yourself, listen back and judge whether it matches the native speaker. The class recording on Canvas also works as a source.

ONE word was ordered onto the vocabulary list by name: taHt, 'under'. 'Let me teach you this word. I need you to add it to your vocab list... I need you to learn this word.' Its dotted twin taxt, 'bed', was explicitly marked optional - 'If you want to learn this, that's optional. But that's because they mentioned it.' Same skeleton, different dot, different sound, different meaning.

Jiim was already taught on Tuesday - she did not remember and had to ask the class. 'Did we bring this one on Tuesday? I thought you were Gene. Oh, I did? Okay, good. Then I can move on... I'm teaching 3 sections, so I don't know where I stopped at each one.' Today's jiim segment was therefore a three-minute review, not new material, and the real new content was Haa and Khaa.

off_slide: Opened on a student request for slang and gave three: shu fi ma fi ('what's up', literally 'what is in, what is not in'), kiif Haalak / kiif Haalik, and yalla - which she pointed out she says constantly in class without translating it. Her test for whether it landed: 'If you say it to any Arab, they will say, oh, you have a Syrian teacher.'
The alphabet-has-an-emoji bit: taa marbuuTa drawn as a smiley face, offered as the students' 'first slang'
Prayer specifically for courage to SPEAK and for enjoyment of the language while speaking, plus learning from mistakes - she asked for prayer requests first and got none

The gym analogy for throat sounds, used twice and meant literally: 'sounding the sounds is exactly like going to the gym and working on your muscles. Here, you're not using this muscle. You didn't use it properly before, or rarely used it before.' She has the class treat Haa as a muscle to be trained over weeks, not a fact to be learned
Two physical images for the Haa constriction: fogging a mirror or eyeglasses before wiping them, and the noise a Syrian makes over hot sweet tea or when cold

Anatomical vocabulary imported from biology - she named the epiglottis for Haa and the soft palate for Khaa, and had students put a hand on the throat to feel that Haa has airflow and constriction but no vibration

Parker asked whether she is deliberately over-emphasising the sounds when she models them, because he did not want to learn an exaggerated pronunciation. Her answer: yes, she is saying them 'forcefully, a little bit more than usual, in order to help you develop your listening skills. When we speak, we speak faster, so we don't make those distinctions' - and in real speech you recover the letter from knowing the word, not from hearing the contrast
Parker was called to the board for drill 2, and also asked the two logistics questions that produced the phone-recording workaround and the Shami-only ruling

Habiib / Habiiba as a register lesson rather than a vocabulary item: fine to a child, fine husband to wife or between engaged couples, 'inappropriate in a formal setting'. The feminine Habiiba she called 'more casual and... genderless', with Habiib the proper masculine
The plum-versus-peach aside on xawx: the Alif Baa authors are Palestinian, so the book's glosses for xawx and its neighbour are swapped relative to Syrian, Lebanese and Jordanian usage
jiib in Shami means 'bring' (also 'buy'), and sounds almost exactly like English 'jeep' - which is where a drill word led

A student asked about the shadda ('the squiggly thing') before it has been taught; she explained it as doubling a letter into a single emphasised sound and noted Hebrew has the same device, then moved on

A student asked what the Arabic instruction line at the top of the practice slide said; she translated it on the fly and explained these decks were built for heritage speakers who can already speak but cannot read or write - 'Here we have the opposite position'

She reads the class its own scoreboard on pronunciation without softening it - 'I'm still hearing some saying nexla... you're hitting above where you're supposed to hit', and 'I think the Haa and the Khaa need a little bit more practice from my experience with other students'

notes: TWO DATED THINGS, AND THE NEAR ONE IS TIGHT: homework 3 is due Friday 2026-09-11, which is the day after this lecture. She said only 'tomorrow' with no clock time, so 23:59 is the conservative read, and it matches the ledger's other Khouri homework (HW8 due Fri 10/23). Split into two commitments on purpose - the handwritten drills go to Canvas and drill 3 is answered inside Lingco, and a single checkbox pointed at one platform is how the other half gets missed.

The oral assessment re-states the commitment already recorded from the 2026-09-08 lecture, but two fields are now firmer: the platform is Lingco (the 9/8 record could only say 'other'), and 'Tuesday by the end of the day' confirms 23:59 rather than class time. If the downstream due list dedupes, prefer this record's version.

The Egyptian-versus-Shami ruling came from Parker's own question and is now on the record from the professor's mouth: Shami only, Egyptian not wanted. That is the same boundary the Anki build already enforces, and this is the citation for it.

Only one word was ordered onto the vocabulary list by name - taHt. Everything else today was letters and sounds. If a card gets made out of this hour, the highest-value ones are the three-way dot contrast (jiim/Haa/Khaa on one skeleton), the naHla/naxla and naHiil/naxiil minimal pairs, and taHt versus taxt - all four are the same lesson, that in this alphabet the dot IS the word.

She sent the class to PAGE 49 for the Haa reading and listening exercise 2. The ledger maps unit 3 to Alif Baa pages 58-77 and unit 2 to 32-57, so 49 sits in unit 2's printed range. This is either the printed-versus-physical page offset or the Concourse table's known sloppiness, which the ledger itself flags as drifting a week in this stretch. Recorded as spoken, not reconciled, and left out of assigned_reading because she named a page to work in class rather than a reading to do.

Jiim was taught Tuesday 9/8 and repeated today only because she lost track across her three sections. The 9/8 record already carries jiim; do not count today as a second new letter. Net new letters this week: Haa and Khaa.

Roughly twelve of seventy-six minutes went to homework and oral-assessment logistics, and another twenty-one to writing practice at the board. Actual new phonetics was about thirty-two minutes across the two letters. This is a mechanics-heavy hour, which is why the commitments matter more than the content here.

Transcript garbles read through rather than quoted - Teams handles Arabic very badly. Letter names: 'Gene'/'gym'/'G'/'the G' = jiim; 'how'/'ha'/'half'/'haz'/'the hey' = Haa; 'shop'/'cop'/'Cop'/'car'/'call'/'the clock' = khaa. Platform: 'lango'/'lingo'/'Lingo' = Lingco. Assignment: 'ignition drills' = recognition drills. Slang: 'Shufi Mafi'/'Shafi Mafi' = shu fi ma fi; 'Kifhalla'/'Kifilhal'/'kifik' = kiif Haalak / kiif Haalik. Words: 'Heather'/'Hey there' = Hibr; 'Cus' = xass; 'Falah' = fallaaH; 'Naheel' = both naHiil and naxiil depending on the sentence; 'the boo'/'Taboo'/'Debu' = a Haa word with sukuun that the audio never resolves; 'hoboob'/'Haboob' and 'Sisana' and 'toots'/'the boot' and 'Shuben' and 'Jacob'/'Jam' and 'Goodar'/'Kasab' are unrecoverable and were left out of the term list rather than guessed.

Where a garbled word could not be resolved it was dropped, not reconstructed. In particular the last fifteen minutes of board work (drills 1 and 2) is almost entirely single-word utterances from students and is close to unreadable in the transcript; the only recoverable items are jiib, Habiib and a wall word. Nothing was carded from that stretch.

One exchange near 00:56 about a vowel - 'for now, it's how, but I'm going to teach you why, not ooh. That's the second week... next week' - is too garbled to state what she is deferring. Flagged rather than smoothed over. If it matters it will resurface Tuesday.
